title: `list_deliveries` reads any organization's deliveries by id
what_is_wrong: The query filters on the caller-supplied `endpoint_id` alone and never joins or checks `WebhookEndpoint.org_id == user.org_id`, while the two sibling handlers in the same file (`list_api_keys`, `list_webhook_endpoints`) both scope by `org_id`.

title: the signing secret is returned by the list API and written to the log
what_is_wrong: `to_dict()` embeds the raw signing secret, and it is the serializer used by `GET /v1/settings/webhook-endpoints`, so the secret is readable forever by anyone who can call the list route — directly contradicting `docs/webhooks.md` ("the response is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards") — while `send_once` logs the whole header dict, putting the derived signature into application logs on every delivery.

title: signing secrets come from `random`, not a CSPRNG
what_is_wrong: The secret is built from `random.choice`, i.e. the Mersenne Twister, which is seeded from process state and whose internal state is recoverable from a modest amount of observed output, so the secrets are predictable rather than unguessable (the constant is also mis-named: `SECRET_BYTES = 32` selects 32 *characters* from a 62-symbol alphabet, and `tests/webhooks/test_delivery.py::test_new_signing_secret_has_prefix_and_length` pins that character count, cementing the wrong unit).

title: `verify` compares signatures with `==`
what_is_wrong: The HMAC comparison uses Python's short-circuiting `str.__eq__` instead of `hmac.compare_digest`, which is RS1 exactly — a credential comparison without a constant-time helper.

title: the signature is not bound to the timestamp, so the documented replay window cannot be enforced
what_is_wrong: `sign` returns a timestamp but computes the MAC over the payload only, while `docs/webhooks.md` states the signature is "the HMAC-SHA256 of `\"{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}\"`"; `verify` likewise ignores the timestamp entirely, so `X-Acme-Timestamp` is unauthenticated attacker-controlled data.

title: the bytes that are signed are not the bytes that are sent
what_is_wrong: The MAC is computed over `signing.serialize()` output (`json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)`, which uses the `", "`/`": "` separators and sorts keys) while httpx re-serializes the same dict independently for `json=` (compact separators, insertion order), so the transmitted body differs from the signed string — this is R40's producer/strict-consumer divergence, with the receiver's HMAC check as the strict consumer.

file: `app/api/routes/settings.py` — `create_webhook_endpoint`, `if not parsed.scheme.startswith("http") or not parsed.netloc`; `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `httpx.AsyncClient(..., follow_redirects=True)`
title: endpoint URLs are unvalidated against SSRF, and the delivery client follows redirects
what_is_wrong: The check is a surface-form test on the scheme string (R47) rather than a decision about the resolved destination — `startswith("http")` admits `http`, `httpx`, `httpfoo`, contradicting the doc's "Only `https://` URLs are accepted" — and nothing rejects loopback, link-local (`169.254.169.254`), or RFC1918 hosts, while `follow_redirects=True` lets a public-looking host redirect the worker into the internal network.

title: the migration's status CHECK constraint rejects the status the code writes
what_is_wrong: The migration enumerates `'failed'` while both `app/webhooks/models.py::STATUSES` and the two `_finish` call sites use `'failed_permanent'` — the same enum is spelled three times (SQL literal, Python tuple, inline string literal) and one copy drifted (R2/R3, and `STATUSES` is currently dead code that nothing validates against).

title: `UNIQUE (event_id)` makes fan-out to a second endpoint fail
what_is_wrong: One event fans out to every matching endpoint — `enqueue_for_event` builds one `WebhookDelivery` per endpoint with the same `event_id` — but the unique index permits only one row per event, so the intended dedup key (`endpoint_id`, `event_id`) was written as `event_id` alone.

title: `time.sleep` inside an async coroutine blocks the whole event loop
what_is_wrong: `deliver` is `async` and is run under `asyncio.gather`, but the retry backoff uses the blocking `time.sleep` instead of `await asyncio.sleep`, so the sleeping coroutine holds the loop thread.

file: `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `_claim_batch` (`return rows` inside `with session_scope()`), and `deliver` (`endpoint` fetched in one `session_scope`, then read in `send_once`)
title: ORM instances are used after their session closes
what_is_wrong: Both functions return or retain SQLAlchemy instances past the end of their `session_scope`, and every subsequent attribute read — `delivery.attempts`, `delivery.payload`, `delivery.id`, `endpoint.signing_secret`, `endpoint.url` — is a lazy load against a closed session; `_claim_batch` additionally sets `row.status = "in_flight"` and returns the rows from inside the block, so the caller receives instances whose identity map is gone.

title: no test exercises the signature contract the docs tell receivers to implement
what_is_wrong: The transport test asserts only the *shape* of the header (`startswith("sha256=")`, `.isdigit()`) and never that the transmitted body verifies, while `test_verify_accepts_signature_produced_by_sign` is near-tautological because `verify` is implemented as `sign` plus a comparison — so the production primitive that matters (a receiver verifying our request) is never on any test's call path (RT5, Critical because signature verification is a security control).

title: the Redis lock is a check-then-set race and is released by non-owners
what_is_wrong: `get` followed by `set` is not atomic, so two workers polling simultaneously both observe an empty key and both proceed; `expire` is a separate round-trip, so a crash between `set` and `expire` leaves a permanent lock; and the unconditional `delete` in `finally` lets a worker whose 60-second TTL already lapsed delete the lock a *different* worker now holds.

title: `in_flight` has no exit path, so a crashed or cancelled batch wedges deliveries forever
what_is_wrong: `in_flight` is entered on claim and left only by `_finish` on the success or exhausted-retry path; a worker crash, a lock expiry, a `gather` that raises and abandons its siblings, or the CHECK-violation above leaves rows in `in_flight` with nothing that ever reclaims them, and `_claim_batch` filters strictly on `status == "pending"` (R38 clause 1: a transient state with no failure-exit and no bounded timeout).

title: retry policy contradicts the documented contract in three places
what_is_wrong: The docs say "a 4xx is permanent and we stop immediately" but `deliver` retries every non-2xx identically; the docs say "backoff is exponential with jitter" but `backoff_for` is deterministic `2**attempt`; and the docs describe the schedule as if it were driven by `next_attempt_at`, which the in-process loop never reads (R29/R49 — prose claiming behaviour the implementation does not have).

title: naive and aware datetimes are mixed, and the migration columns have no time zone
what_is_wrong: `enqueue_for_event` writes a naive `utcnow()` while `_claim_batch` filters against an aware `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` and `models.py` declares every column `DateTime(timezone=True)`, but the migration creates them as `TIMESTAMP` (without time zone) — three descriptions of one column that do not agree (R3: the aware-datetime pattern was applied in `models.py::_now` and in `_claim_batch` but not in `enqueue_for_event` or the DDL).

title: the dispatcher swallows enqueue failures and enqueues outside the event's transaction
what_is_wrong: The enqueue runs after the event's `session_scope` has already committed, in its own transaction, and every failure is downgraded to `log.warning` — so a failed enqueue leaves a committed event with no delivery rows and no retry (R9: fire-and-forget dispatch outside the transaction boundary; R36: a broad catch standing in for a fix).

file: `app/events/dispatcher.py` — `WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES`; `docs/webhooks.md` — "An empty `event_types` subscribes the endpoint to every event type we emit"
title: `WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES` is a hardcoded three-element allowlist that contradicts the documented "every event type"
what_is_wrong: The dispatcher enqueues only for three literal event types, so an endpoint with `event_types: []` receives those three and nothing else, and an endpoint that explicitly subscribes to any other type receives nothing at all — the member set was anchored on a supplied list rather than derived from the events the system actually emits (R42), and neither the API nor `enqueue_for_event` validates a requested type against it.

file: `migrations/0042_webhook_delivery.sql` — `ALTER TABLE organizations ADD COLUMN webhooks_enabled BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE`
title: `webhooks_enabled` is added to `organizations` and never read
what_is_wrong: The column declares a per-organization capability gate, but no code in the diff reads it — `create_webhook_endpoint` accepts registrations and `enqueue_for_event` fans out regardless (R41: a declared capability with no backing path).

title: the three new routes have no rate limiting
what_is_wrong: None of the new endpoints carries a rate-limit dependency (RS2), and the create route is the more expensive of the two because each call performs a DNS resolution once the SSRF fix lands and mints a secret.

title: `limit` on the deliveries route has a floor but no ceiling
what_is_wrong: `ge=1` bounds only the lower end, so `?limit=100000000` is accepted and passed straight to `.limit()` (RS3: the parameter is only half-validated at the schema layer).

file: `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `_finish`, `row = session.get(...)` then `row.status = status`; and `_finish(delivery.id, "delivered", attempt, response.status_code, response.text)`
title: `_finish` dereferences a possibly-`None` row and stores the response body unbounded
what_is_wrong: `session.get` returns `None` for a deleted row and the next line dereferences it unguarded, and the `detail` written into `response_body` is the receiver's entire untruncated response text.

title: `run_worker` can reference an unbound `batch`, and `gather` abandons siblings on the first exception
what_is_wrong: `batch` is assigned inside the `try`, but `if not batch` is evaluated after the `finally`, so an exception in `_claim_batch` raises `NameError` (masking the real error) — and `asyncio.gather` without `return_exceptions=True` propagates the first failure while the sibling coroutines are left unawaited.

title: new production exports ship with no test coverage
what_is_wrong: `tests/webhooks/test_delivery.py` imports only `MAX_ATTEMPTS`, `backoff_for` and `send_once`, so of the twelve new callable surfaces exactly one is exercised (RT6); the untested set is precisely where the Critical findings above live — the detached-instance bug, the lock race, the CHECK-constraint violation and the tenancy hole are all in code no test calls.

title: test doubles diverge from the real boundary in exactly the property under test
what_is_wrong: Both doubles are plain classes with class-level attributes, so they have none of the properties of the SQLAlchemy models they stand in for — no session affinity, no lazy loading, no JSONB round-trip — which is why the detached-instance defect and the naive/aware timestamp defect are invisible to a green suite (RT1: the mock's shape matches while the behaviour under test does not).

title: `event_types` is stored without validation of its element type
what_is_wrong: The declaration bounds neither the list length nor the individual string length, so a tenant can store a multi-megabyte JSONB array that `enqueue_for_event` then scans (`event_type in endpoint.event_types`) on every dispatch.

title: the claim query has no supporting index
what_is_wrong: `_claim_batch` filters on `status` and `next_attempt_at` and sorts by `next_attempt_at`, but only `status` is indexed, and `webhook_endpoints.org_id` — the column both list routes filter on — has no index at all.

title: `STATUSES` is declared and never used
what_is_wrong: The tuple is defined but referenced nowhere, so it neither constrains the `status` column nor is checked against the migration's CHECK list — which is how the `failed` / `failed_permanent` divergence survived.

file: `docs/webhooks.md` — "returns the most recent attempts for an endpoint belonging to your organization"
title: the docs describe an endpoint-scoping guarantee the route does not implement
what_is_wrong: The sentence asserts the tenancy scoping that `list_deliveries` omits, so the prose is the only place the control exists (R49 — a claim stronger than the implementation).

title: the signature is computed over bytes that are never sent, so no customer can ever verify a delivery
what_is_wrong: `sign()` HMACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` (sorted keys, `", "`/`": "` separators) while `send_once()` sends the body via `client.post(..., json=delivery.payload)`, which httpx serializes with insertion order and compact separators — two different byte strings — and the signed input omits the timestamp entirely, though `docs/webhooks.md` tells integrators the MAC covers `"{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}"`.

title: signature comparison is not constant-time (RS1)
what_is_wrong: the HMAC comparison uses Python's `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte, and the diff ships this as the reference verifier while `docs/webhooks.md` instructs customers to "compare … using a constant-time comparison".

title: signing secrets are generated with the non-cryptographic `random` module
what_is_wrong: the secret is built from `random.choice(_ALPHABET)`, i.e. the Mersenne Twister PRNG seeded from process state, which is fully reconstructible from ~624 observed outputs and is never acceptable for key material.

title: the signing secret is returned on every endpoint read and written to the application log
what_is_wrong: `to_dict()` unconditionally includes `signing_secret`, so `GET /v1/settings/webhook-endpoints` hands the secret back on every call — directly contradicting `docs/webhooks.md` ("the response is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards") — and `send_once` logs the full header dict including the computed `X-Acme-Signature` (RS4: live credential material in a committed/shipped artifact).

title: the deliveries endpoint is not scoped to the caller's organization (R3 — the tenancy predicate is applied at two of three new routes)
what_is_wrong: the query filters only on `WebhookDelivery.endpoint_id == endpoint_id` and never joins to `WebhookEndpoint` to check `org_id == user.org_id`, while the two sibling routes added in the same diff (`list_webhook_endpoints`, and `create_webhook_endpoint` which stamps `org_id=user.org_id`) do apply the tenancy predicate.

title: the migration's status CHECK constraint does not contain the terminal status the code writes
what_is_wrong: the same enum is spelled in two places with different members (R2: constants duplicated, and here they are not even value-equal), so the exhausted-retry path writes a value the database rejects.

file: `migrations/0042_webhook_delivery.sql` — `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_webhook_deliveries_event ON webhook_deliveries (event_id)`; producer `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `enqueue_for_event`
title: the unique index on `event_id` makes any org with more than one endpoint undeliverable
what_is_wrong: `enqueue_for_event` inserts one row per matching endpoint for a single `event_id`, but the index permits only one row per `event_id` across the entire table.

title: the worker mutates and reads ORM instances after their session has closed
what_is_wrong: `_claim_batch` sets `row.status = "in_flight"` and returns the ORM objects, but the `with session_scope()` block exits before the return value is used, so every later access — `delivery.attempts`, `delivery.id`, `delivery.payload` in `deliver`/`send_once` — touches a detached, expired-on-commit instance.

title: `time.sleep()` inside an async coroutine blocks the whole event loop
what_is_wrong: the retry backoff uses the blocking `time.sleep` inside an `async def` that `run_worker` schedules through `asyncio.gather`, so the sleeping coroutine freezes the event loop instead of yielding it.

title: `in_flight` is a non-terminal state with no timeout and no reset path (R38)
what_is_wrong: rows are moved to `in_flight` before delivery, `_claim_batch` only ever selects `status == "pending"`, and nothing anywhere returns an `in_flight` row to `pending`, so any worker crash, redeploy, or unhandled exception (all of the Critical findings above produce one) strands the row permanently.

title: outbound URLs are unrestricted and redirects are followed — server-side request forgery
what_is_wrong: the only destination check is `scheme.startswith("http") and netloc`, so `http://127.0.0.1:6379/`, `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`, and any RFC 1918 address are accepted; and even a legitimately-registered public host can 302 the worker to those targets because the client follows redirects.

title: boundary validation is superficial and contradicts the published contract (RS3)
what_is_wrong: `parsed.scheme.startswith("http")` accepts `httpfoo://` and plain `http://` although `docs/webhooks.md` states "Only `https://` URLs are accepted"; `event_types: list[str]` is accepted verbatim with no membership check against any known event set; `url` has no length bound; and `limit: int = Query(50, ge=1)` has no upper bound.

title: the Redis "lock" is not atomic and is released by whoever finishes, not by its owner
what_is_wrong: `get` then `set` is a check-then-act race with no `NX`, the `set` and `expire` are two separate round-trips (a crash between them leaves a permanent lock), and the `finally` deletes the key unconditionally without checking the holder token, so a worker whose 60 s TTL already expired deletes the *next* worker's lock.

title: the webhook enqueue is fire-and-forget outside the event transaction, and its failures are swallowed (R9)
what_is_wrong: the `Event` row is committed by its own `session_scope`, then `enqueue_for_event` opens a *second* transaction, and any failure of that second transaction is caught by a bare `except Exception` and downgraded to a warning that returns `event_id` as if everything succeeded.

file: `app/events/dispatcher.py` — `WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES`; `migrations/0042_webhook_delivery.sql` — `ALTER TABLE organizations ADD COLUMN webhooks_enabled BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE`; `docs/webhooks.md`
title: the deliverable event set is a hardcoded triple that contradicts the documented contract, and `webhooks_enabled` is declared but never read (R4 / R18 / R41)
what_is_wrong: `docs/webhooks.md` promises that an empty `event_types` "subscribes the endpoint to every event type we emit", but `dispatch` only calls `enqueue_for_event` for three literal types, so every other emitted event is dropped before `enqueue_for_event`'s own per-endpoint filter is ever consulted; and the new `webhooks_enabled` column is read by no code in the diff, so the capability it declares has no backing path and the feature is in fact on for every org regardless of the flag (R41).

title: the documentation describes four behaviours the implementation does not have (R49 / R29)
what_is_wrong: the doc states backoff is "exponential with jitter" (`backoff_for` has no jitter), that "a 4xx is permanent and we stop immediately" (`deliver` retries every non-2xx status equally), that only `https://` URLs are accepted (the handler accepts `http://`), and that the signing secret "cannot be read back afterwards" (`to_dict` returns it on every list) — four claims stronger than the code, in a document customers integrate against.

title: naive and aware datetimes are mixed, and the migration's columns are not `timestamptz`
what_is_wrong: `datetime.utcnow()` returns a naive value written into a column the ORM declares as timezone-aware while the DDL declares it without a zone, and it is later compared against an aware `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` in the claim query.

title: the entire delivery pipeline ships without tests (RT6 / RT5)
what_is_wrong: the diff adds `enqueue_for_event`, `deliver`, `run_worker`, `_acquire_lock`, `_claim_batch`, `_finish`, three HTTP routes, and two models, and the test file exercises exactly one of them plus two pure functions — so the retry loop, the state machine, the distributed lock, and the tenancy predicate all ship unexercised, and per RT5 the constants test (`MAX_ATTEMPTS == 5`) asserts a number without ever driving the loop that consumes it.

title: the delivery test's doubles and its signature assertion cannot detect the signature defect (RT1)
what_is_wrong: the test asserts only that the header *starts with* `sha256=` and that the timestamp header `isdigit()` — it never recomputes the MAC over `captured["body"]` — and the doubles are hand-rolled classes rather than the real `WebhookEndpoint`/`WebhookDelivery`, so no field of the real model is bound by the type system (RT1 (a)) and the assertion compares two outputs of the subject rather than an independently derived expected value (RT1 (c)/(d)).

title: `_finish` dereferences a possibly-absent row and stores an unbounded response body
what_is_wrong: `session.get` returns `None` for a deleted delivery (its endpoint may have been cascade-deleted mid-flight) and the next line dereferences it, and `detail` is `response.text` verbatim with no size cap into a `TEXT` column that `list_deliveries` then returns to the caller.

title: the three new routes have no rate limiting (RS2)
what_is_wrong: none of the new endpoints carries a rate-limit dependency, and `create_webhook_endpoint` performs an unbounded write that also generates a secret on every call.

title: deliveries are ordered by a non-total key and paged with `limit` (R57)
what_is_wrong: both queries order by a wall-clock timestamp that ties freely — `enqueue_for_event` stamps every row of one fan-out with the same `next_attempt_at`, and `created_at` defaults to the same `_now()` for a batch — while taking a `LIMIT`, so the rows returned at the cut are undefined.

title: the delivery index does not cover the claim query
what_is_wrong: `_claim_batch` filters on `status` *and* `next_attempt_at` and orders by `next_attempt_at`, but the index covers `status` alone, which is a low-cardinality column.

title: the backoff test hardcodes the schedule instead of deriving it from the constant (RT3)
what_is_wrong: the expected values are literals rather than derived from `BASE_DELAY_SECONDS`, and `test_max_attempts_matches_documented_limit` asserts `MAX_ATTEMPTS == 5` against another literal.

title: `backoff_for(0)` returns 1 second and the first retry uses `attempt=1`
what_is_wrong: the function is defined over all integers but only 1..4 are meaningful; `backoff_for(0)` is 1 s and `backoff_for(5)` (reachable if `MAX_ATTEMPTS` is raised) is 32 s with no ceiling.

title: `enqueue_for_event` is declared `async` but performs only blocking synchronous DB work
what_is_wrong: the coroutine contains no `await`, so `dispatch`'s `await` yields nothing and the synchronous SQLAlchemy calls run on the event loop thread.

title: the signature is computed over bytes that are not the bytes sent on the wire
what_is_wrong: `sign()` HMACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` (sorted keys, `", "`/`": "` separators) while `send_once` transmits the body httpx produces from `json=delivery.payload` (insertion order, compact separators), so the signed string and the request body are different byte sequences for any payload whose keys are not already sorted — the diff's own fixture `{"id": "evt_1", "type": "invoice.paid", "amount_cents": 4200}` signs `{"amount_cents": 4200, "id": ...}` and sends `{"id":"evt_1",...}`.

title: the timestamp header is not covered by the signature, so the documented replay window is not enforceable
what_is_wrong: `sign()` returns a timestamp but HMACs only the payload, and `verify()` recomputes with a *fresh* `time.time()` that it then discards, so the timestamp is unauthenticated and unchecked — an attacker who captures one request can replay it forever with any timestamp value.

title: signature comparison is not constant-time (RS1)
what_is_wrong: the shipped verifier compares an HMAC digest with Python's `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte.

title: signing secrets are generated from a non-cryptographic PRNG
what_is_wrong: `random` is the Mersenne Twister, whose internal state is recoverable from observed output, so secrets are predictable rather than unguessable.

title: every endpoint list response returns the signing secret, contradicting the documented one-time disclosure
what_is_wrong: `to_dict()` includes `signing_secret`, and `GET /v1/settings/webhook-endpoints` returns it for every endpoint, while `docs/webhooks.md` states the creation response "is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards".

title: `list_deliveries` is not scoped to the caller's organization (IDOR)
what_is_wrong: the query filters on the path-supplied `endpoint_id` only and never joins to `WebhookEndpoint.org_id == user.org_id`, unlike its sibling `list_webhook_endpoints` two functions above which does filter on `org_id` — the tenancy predicate present on the neighbouring route was not propagated (R3).

file: `app/events/dispatcher.py` — `WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES`, and the `if envelope.type in WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES` guard
title: `WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES` is a second, hardcoded allowlist that silently overrides customer subscriptions
what_is_wrong: delivery is gated by a three-element set hardcoded in the dispatcher *and* by `endpoint.event_types` in `enqueue_for_event`, so the customer-facing subscription list is not the deciding one (R18/R42: the class of deliverable events was anchored on a supplied list rather than derived).

title: the Redis lock is not atomic, is not owned, and expires before the work it guards
what_is_wrong: `get`-then-`set` is a check-then-act race, `set` and `expire` are two round trips (a crash between them leaves the lock permanently held with no TTL), the lock carries no owner token so any worker's `finally` deletes whoever's lock is currently held, and the 60-second TTL is shorter than a batch of 100 deliveries at a 30-second request timeout.

file: `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `_claim_batch` sets `status = "in_flight"`, and no code ever moves a row out of it except `_finish`
title: `in_flight` is a non-terminal state with no reset path (R38)
what_is_wrong: every path that fails between claim and finish — worker crash, deploy, the CHECK violation above, `DetachedInstanceError`, a cancelled task — leaves the row `in_flight` forever, and `_claim_batch` only ever selects `status == "pending"`.

title: the worker loop dies on the first unhandled exception
what_is_wrong: `_claim_batch`, `asyncio.gather(...)` and the Redis calls are inside a `try` whose only clause is `finally`, so any database blip, `IntegrityError`, or per-delivery exception propagates out of `while True` and terminates the worker.

file: `app/events/dispatcher.py` — `except Exception as exc: log.warning("webhook enqueue failed for event %s: %s", event_id, exc)`
title: the dispatcher swallows every webhook enqueue failure (R9/R4)
what_is_wrong: the enqueue runs after the event transaction has already committed and its failures are caught, downgraded to a WARNING, and discarded — there is no outbox row, no retry, and no counter, so the event exists with no delivery record and nothing will ever notice.

title: unbounded and unvalidated request parameters on the three new routes (RS3)
what_is_wrong: `url` is a bare `str` validated by hand after parsing rather than at the schema level, `event_types` is an unbounded `list[str]` of arbitrary strings written straight into a JSONB column, and `limit` has a lower bound but no upper bound.

title: no rate limiting on any of the three new routes (RS2)
what_is_wrong: three new authenticated routes are added with no rate limiter and no per-organization quota, and endpoint creation in particular has an amplification factor — each endpoint multiplies the outbound POSTs we make per event.

file: `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `_finish(..., detail=response.text)` on both the success and failure paths, and `log.info("POST %s headers=%s", endpoint.url, headers)` in `send_once`
title: full response bodies from customer endpoints are stored unbounded, and every request's headers are logged
what_is_wrong: `response.text` is written into `response_body` with no size cap and no content-type check, and the INFO log line prints the full header dict including `X-Acme-Signature` on every single attempt.

title: newly added production symbols ship with no tests (RT6)
what_is_wrong: the test file covers only `sign`, `verify`, `new_signing_secret`, `backoff_for`, `MAX_ATTEMPTS` and `send_once`; `enqueue_for_event`, `deliver`, `_claim_batch`, `_acquire_lock`, `run_worker`, `_finish`, both model `to_dict` methods, and all three HTTP routes have no test at all.

title: the test fakes diverge from the ORM objects the production path actually holds (RT1)
what_is_wrong: `FakeDelivery` exposes only `id`, `attempts` and `payload` as plain class attributes on a live object, whereas production passes a *detached* `WebhookDelivery` whose attribute access raises, and `FakeEndpoint` omits `active`, `event_types` and `org_id` entirely.

title: `test_new_signing_secret_has_prefix_and_length` cannot fail for a non-random generator (RT7)
what_is_wrong: the only assertions are the prefix and the length, both of which a generator returning the constant `"whsec_" + "a" * 32` satisfies — the test reads as coverage of secret generation while being blind to the property that matters.

file: `docs/webhooks.md` — "backoff is exponential with jitter, roughly 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s", vs `app/webhooks/delivery.py::backoff_for`
title: `backoff_for` has no jitter although the docs promise it
what_is_wrong: `backoff_for` is deterministic `2**attempt`, so a mass failure produces a synchronized retry thundering herd against the recovering endpoint.

title: the retry table in the docs stops one attempt short of the code
what_is_wrong: five attempts means four waits ending at 32s under `2**attempt` for `attempt=5`, and `test_backoff_grows_exponentially` parametrizes only attempts 1–4, so the last interval is neither documented nor tested.

title: no index supports the claim query or the delivery listing
what_is_wrong: the claim query filters `status = 'pending' AND next_attempt_at <= now()` ordered by `next_attempt_at`, and `list_deliveries` filters `endpoint_id` ordered by `created_at DESC`, neither of which the single low-cardinality `status` index serves.

title: `endpoint.active` is checked at enqueue time but never at send time
what_is_wrong: a row enqueued while the endpoint was active is still delivered after the endpoint is deactivated, since nothing consults `active` between claim and POST.

title: `serialize()` leaves `ensure_ascii` and `separators` at their defaults
what_is_wrong: only `sort_keys` is pinned, so the canonical form still depends on the running Python's `json` defaults for whitespace and non-ASCII escaping.

title: the signature is computed over bytes that are never sent, so no customer can ever verify a delivery
what_is_wrong: `sign()` HMACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` while the request body is produced independently by `client.post(..., json=delivery.payload)`, which serializes with httpx's own `json.dumps` (insertion key order, `", "`/`": "` separators), and the timestamp that `docs/webhooks.md` says is part of the MAC input (`"{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}"`) is not fed into the HMAC at all.

title: signing secrets are generated from `random`, not a CSPRNG
what_is_wrong: `random.choice` draws from the module-global Mersenne Twister, which is not cryptographically secure and whose internal state is recoverable from a modest run of outputs.

title: `GET /v1/settings/webhook-endpoints` returns every endpoint's signing secret
what_is_wrong: `to_dict()` unconditionally includes `signing_secret`, and the list route returns it for every endpoint, directly contradicting `docs/webhooks.md` ("The response is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards"), which is R49's claim-stronger-than-implementation with the doc as the overstated control.

title: `list_deliveries` has no tenancy filter — any authenticated user can read any organization's webhook payloads
what_is_wrong: the query filters only on `WebhookDelivery.endpoint_id` taken straight from the path, with no join back to `WebhookEndpoint.org_id == user.org_id`, while both sibling routes in the same file (`list_api_keys`, `list_webhook_endpoints`) do filter by `user.org_id` — the pattern was propagated to two of three new call sites (R3, cross-cutting).

title: the migration's status CHECK constraint rejects the status the code writes
what_is_wrong: the schema allows `'failed'` while `models.STATUSES` and `_finish(delivery.id, "failed_permanent", ...)` use `'failed_permanent'` — the enum spelling was changed in the Python layer and not propagated to the migration (R3/R2/R18), and `STATUSES` is declared but never bound to a `CheckConstraint`, so nothing cross-checks the two lists.

title: `UNIQUE INDEX ... (event_id)` makes fan-out to a second endpoint impossible
what_is_wrong: the uniqueness key is `event_id` alone, but `enqueue_for_event` creates one `WebhookDelivery` row per matching endpoint for a single `event_id`, so `session.add_all(rows)` violates the index as soon as an org has two subscribed endpoints.

title: `time.sleep()` inside an `async def` blocks the whole event loop during retry backoff
what_is_wrong: `deliver` is a coroutine gathered concurrently by `run_worker`, but its backoff uses the blocking `time.sleep`, and the surrounding `session_scope()` DB work is synchronous too.

title: ORM objects are used after their session closes, so the worker cannot deliver anything
what_is_wrong: `_claim_batch` returns `WebhookDelivery` instances after the `with session_scope()` block exits, and `deliver` loads `endpoint` inside a scope and then reads `endpoint.signing_secret` / `endpoint.url` and `delivery.payload` / `.id` / `.attempts` outside it; with SQLAlchemy's default `expire_on_commit=True` those attributes are expired and the instances detached.

title: SSRF — any URL is accepted, redirects are followed, and the response body is stored and readable
what_is_wrong: `parsed.scheme.startswith("http")` accepts plain `http://` (and anything spelled `httpx://`, `httpfoo://`) against the doc's "Only `https://` URLs are accepted", nothing rejects loopback / link-local / RFC1918 / metadata hosts, `follow_redirects=True` lets a benign-looking public URL redirect the POST to an internal one, and the full response body is written to `response_body`.

title: `verify()` compares signatures with `==`
what_is_wrong: the exported verification helper compares the expected and supplied signatures with a plain `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte (RS1); the function is currently reached only from tests, but it is a public production export documented as the verification recipe.

title: the signature test never verifies a signature, which is why the wire-bytes defect ships green
what_is_wrong: the test asserts only that the header *starts with* `sha256=` and that the timestamp is digits — it never feeds `captured["body"]` back through `signing.verify`, so the production primitive (signature over the actual request bytes) is not on the test's call path at all (RT5); it also substitutes `FakeEndpoint`/`FakeDelivery` for the real models, so nothing checks that `signing_secret`/`payload` are the attributes the ORM actually exposes (RT1).

title: webhook enqueue is fire-and-forget after the event transaction commits, and its failure is swallowed
what_is_wrong: the event row is committed in one transaction and `enqueue_for_event` opens its own afterwards, so any failure between them (and any exception inside, which is caught and downgraded to a warning) loses the fan-out with no retry, no dead-letter, and a `200` returned to the caller (R9).

title: `WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES` silently overrides what customers subscribed to
what_is_wrong: fan-out only happens for three hardcoded types, but the API accepts any string in `event_types` and the docs promise an empty list "subscribes the endpoint to every event type we emit" — the allowlist and the subscription surface are not synchronized (R12/R18), and the doc claim is stronger than the implementation (R49).

title: `_acquire_lock` is a non-atomic check-then-set, and a crash between `set` and `expire` wedges delivery forever
what_is_wrong: `get` followed by `set` is two round-trips with no atomicity so two workers both win, the TTL is applied in a third command so a crash in between leaves a key with no expiry (R38's persisted fail-closed wedge), and the `finally` deletes the key unconditionally — including a lock a *different* worker acquired after this one's TTL lapsed.

title: `in_flight` is a non-terminal state with no reclaim path
what_is_wrong: rows enter `in_flight` at claim time and leave it only via `_finish` on the success or exhausted-retry path, so a worker crash, an OOM kill, a deploy mid-batch, or the CHECK-constraint failure described above strands them permanently, and `_claim_batch` only ever selects `status == "pending"` (R38 case 1).

title: retry policy contradicts the documented policy on both the 4xx rule and jitter
what_is_wrong: the docs state "a 4xx is permanent and we stop immediately" and "backoff is exponential with jitter", but `deliver` retries every non-2xx status (4xx included) up to `MAX_ATTEMPTS` and `backoff_for` returns a deterministic `2**attempt` with no jitter (R29/R49).

title: naive/aware datetime split, and `datetime.utcnow()` reimplements the module's own `_now()` helper
what_is_wrong: `enqueue_for_event` writes a naive `datetime.utcnow()` into a column the model declares `DateTime(timezone=True)` and the migration declares `TIMESTAMP` (without time zone), while `_claim_batch` filters against an aware `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` — and `models.py` already exports `_now()`, the exact helper this line reimplements (R1).

title: `_claim_batch` orders on a non-unique timestamp with no tie-break and no row-level claim
what_is_wrong: `ORDER BY next_attempt_at LIMIT 100` uses a wall-clock value that ties constantly (every delivery from one fan-out shares the same enqueue instant) and there is no `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so the order among tied rows is undefined and two concurrent workers select overlapping sets (R57).

title: `run_worker` dies on the first exception and can raise `NameError` on `batch`
what_is_wrong: `batch` is assigned inside the `try` but read after the `finally`, so any exception from `_claim_batch` or `gather` leaves it unbound and, more importantly, propagates out of the `while True` loop — there is no `except` anywhere in the poll body.

title: full signed request headers are logged at INFO on every attempt
what_is_wrong: the header dict logged in full contains `X-Acme-Signature` and `X-Acme-Timestamp`, and the same function is the natural place a future edit adds an `Authorization` header, so a valid signature for a known payload lands in the log pipeline on every attempt.

title: none of the three new routes has rate limiting, and endpoints per org are unbounded
what_is_wrong: no limiter is applied to any of the three new routes (RS2), and nothing caps how many endpoints an org may register or how large `event_types` may be.

title: `limit` on the deliveries route has a floor but no ceiling
what_is_wrong: `ge=1` bounds the parameter from below only, so `?limit=100000000` is accepted and pushed straight into `.limit()` (RS3 — the validation that exists is half a validation).

title: the delivery worker, the routes, and the enqueue path ship with no tests
what_is_wrong: the diff adds `enqueue_for_event`, `deliver`, `run_worker`, `_acquire_lock`, `_claim_batch`, `_finish`, `WebhookEndpoint`, `WebhookDelivery`, and three routes, and the only exports exercised are `backoff_for`, `MAX_ATTEMPTS`, `send_once`, and the signing helpers (RT6); the retry loop, the lock, the state machine, and the tenancy filter are all untested.

file: `migrations/0042_webhook_delivery.sql` — `ALTER TABLE organizations ADD COLUMN webhooks_enabled BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE`
title: `organizations.webhooks_enabled` is added by the migration and read by nothing
what_is_wrong: the column is created defaulting to FALSE, implying a per-org gate, but no model maps it and neither `create_webhook_endpoint` nor `enqueue_for_event` consults it (R41 — a declared capability with no backing path).

title: `_finish` assumes the row exists and stores an unbounded remote response body
what_is_wrong: `session.get(m.WebhookDelivery, delivery_id)` can return `None` (the endpoint and its deliveries cascade-delete while a batch is in flight) and the very next line dereferences it, and `response_body = detail` writes the customer's entire response text with no cap.

title: `SECRET_BYTES` names bytes but counts characters, and the test cements the misnomer
what_is_wrong: the constant is used as a character count over a 62-symbol alphabet (~190 bits), not a byte count, and the test asserts `len(secret) == len(prefix) + SECRET_BYTES`, which will fail the moment the generator is corrected to `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` (43 characters).

title: `models.STATUSES` is declared but never enforced
what_is_wrong: the tuple is defined at module scope and referenced nowhere, so it documents an invariant that nothing checks — and it is the single place that disagrees with the migration's CHECK list.

title: the deliveries listing has no supporting index
what_is_wrong: `list_deliveries` filters on `endpoint_id` and orders by `created_at DESC`, but the only indexes are on `status` and (uniquely) `event_id`.

title: the signature is computed over different bytes than the ones sent, and the timestamp is not covered by the MAC
what_is_wrong: `sign()` HMACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` (default `", "`/`": "` separators, keys sorted) while the request body is produced independently by `client.post(..., json=delivery.payload)`, which serializes with httpx's own compact, unsorted encoder — so the transmitted body never matches the signed string — and the timestamp header is generated but never fed into the MAC, contradicting `docs/webhooks.md` ("the HMAC-SHA256 of `"{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}"`").

title: `new_signing_secret` derives per-customer HMAC keys from `random`, not a CSPRNG
what_is_wrong: the secret is built from `random.choice`, i.e. the Mersenne Twister PRNG, which is unseeded from entropy in a predictable way and whose internal state is recoverable from a modest number of observed outputs.

title: `GET /webhook-endpoints` returns every endpoint's signing secret, contradicting the documented one-time-disclosure contract
what_is_wrong: `to_dict()` unconditionally includes `"signing_secret"`, and `list_webhook_endpoints` returns it on every read, while `docs/webhooks.md` states the creation response "is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards".

title: signature and timestamp headers are logged at INFO on every delivery attempt
what_is_wrong: the entire header dict, including `X-Acme-Signature` and `X-Acme-Timestamp`, is written to application logs on every attempt.

title: `verify` compares signatures with `==`
what_is_wrong: an HMAC comparison uses Python's short-circuiting `==` instead of a constant-time comparison (RS1).

title: the deliveries endpoint has no tenancy filter — any authenticated user can read any organization's webhook payloads
what_is_wrong: the query filters on `WebhookDelivery.endpoint_id == endpoint_id` only, with no join back to `WebhookEndpoint.org_id == user.org_id`, whereas the sibling `list_webhook_endpoints` added in the same diff *does* filter by `org_id` — an incomplete propagation of the tenancy pattern (R3, security-relevant).

title: endpoint URLs are unvalidated against internal targets, and the delivery client follows redirects — SSRF
what_is_wrong: the only check is `parsed.scheme.startswith("http") and parsed.netloc`, which admits plaintext `http://`, admits any scheme merely *prefixed* with `http` (`httpx://`, `http+unix://`), and blocks no loopback, link-local, or RFC1918 destination; `follow_redirects=True` then means even a validated public HTTPS host can 302 the delivery worker to an internal address.

title: the migration's status CHECK constraint does not include the status the code writes
what_is_wrong: the SQL constraint allows `'failed'` while the model's `STATUSES` tuple and the only writer in `delivery.py` use `'failed_permanent'`; the vocabulary is defined in three unlinked places and `STATUSES` is never actually applied to the column (R2 / R3).

title: the unique index on `event_id` alone allows only one delivery row per event across all endpoints
what_is_wrong: uniqueness is declared on `event_id` by itself, but `enqueue_for_event` inserts one row per matching endpoint for the same `event_id`.

title: `time.sleep` inside an async coroutine blocks the entire event loop through the whole retry ladder
what_is_wrong: `deliver` is `async` and is run under `asyncio.gather`, but the retry backoff uses the blocking `time.sleep`, and the retry loop is inside the delivery coroutine rather than driven by `next_attempt_at` off the queue.

title: the dispatch lock is a non-atomic get-then-set with a separately issued TTL
what_is_wrong: the check-then-set has a window in which two workers both observe an absent key and both proceed; the `expire` is a second round trip so a crash between `set` and `expire` leaves a lock with no TTL; and the release deletes the key unconditionally, including a lock some *other* worker acquired after this one's TTL lapsed (R38: a persisted fail-closed wedge with no reset path, plus fail-open supersession).

title: the worker builds an idempotency contract the payload cannot satisfy — `event_id` is never sent to the receiver
what_is_wrong: the POST body is the raw `delivery.payload` (the event's inner payload), with no envelope carrying `id`, `type`, or `created`, so the documented deduplication key is not present on the wire — and the test fixture's `payload = {"id": "evt_1", "type": "invoice.paid", ...}` invents an envelope shape that production never produces (R40 producer/consumer divergence; RT1 mock-reality divergence, the mock being exactly what hides the gap).

title: the dispatcher swallows every enqueue failure, and enqueue is not atomic with the event write
what_is_wrong: the enqueue runs in its own `session_scope` after the event transaction has committed, and any failure — the unique-index violation above, a Redis or DB blip, a bug — is downgraded to a warning with no retry, no dead-letter, and no signal to the caller (R9/R5: the side effect is not atomic with the mutation it accompanies).

file: `app/events/dispatcher.py` — `WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES`; `docs/webhooks.md` — "An empty `event_types` subscribes the endpoint to every event type we emit"
title: the dispatcher's hardcoded three-event allowlist contradicts the documented "every event type we emit"
what_is_wrong: webhook enqueue is gated on a module-level set of three literal type strings that no other component knows about, while both the docs and `enqueue_for_event`'s own per-endpoint filter (`if not endpoint.event_types or event_type in endpoint.event_types`) promise a universal subscription (R42: the class of deliverable event types is anchored on a hand-supplied list rather than derived from the emitting primitive; R2: the type vocabulary is duplicated).

title: naive and timezone-aware datetimes are mixed across the enqueue/claim boundary, and the migration's columns are timezone-less
what_is_wrong: `enqueue_for_event` writes a naive UTC value while the model declares `DateTime(timezone=True)` and the claim query compares against an aware value, and the SQL columns are `TIMESTAMP` (no zone) with a `now()` default that casts to the session's local time — three inconsistent notions of "when"; the change already ships a `_now()` helper in `models.py` that `enqueue_for_event` does not use (R1/R17 helper adoption, with the evidence being `models._now` in the same diff).

title: `_claim_batch` returns ORM instances after its session closes, and claims without row-level locking
what_is_wrong: the rows are loaded and mutated inside `with session_scope() as session:` and then returned out of that block, so with SQLAlchemy's default `expire_on_commit=True` every attribute `deliver` touches (`delivery.attempts`, `delivery.payload`, `delivery.id`, `delivery.endpoint_id`) triggers a refresh on a closed session and raises `DetachedInstanceError`; separately, the `SELECT` has no `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so the status write is a classic read-then-write TOCTOU (R5) that only the broken lock was standing in for.

title: `in_flight` is a non-terminal state with no reaper, and an unhandled exception permanently kills the worker
what_is_wrong: nothing ever moves a row out of `in_flight` except a successful `_finish`, and `_claim_batch` only selects `status == "pending"`, so any crash, redeploy, or raised exception between claim and finish strands the row forever (R38 non-terminal transient state); `run_worker`'s `while True` has no exception handler, so a single failure inside the loop terminates the worker permanently.

title: no rate limiting on any of the three new endpoints, and `limit` has no upper bound
what_is_wrong: three new public routes ship with no rate limiter (RS2), no cap on how many endpoints an organization may register, and a `limit` constrained only from below, so `?limit=100000000` is accepted (RS3).

title: the claim and listing queries order on non-unique keys, so page boundaries are undefined
what_is_wrong: both queries order on a wall-clock timestamp with a LIMIT, and ties are the norm here rather than the edge case — every row `enqueue_for_event` creates in one call shares an identical `next_attempt_at`, and rows created in one batch share `created_at` (R57).

title: retry semantics and backoff jitter documented but not implemented
what_is_wrong: the docs state "a 4xx is permanent and we stop immediately" and "backoff is exponential with jitter", but `deliver` retries every non-2xx status identically up to `MAX_ATTEMPTS` and `backoff_for` is a pure power of two with no jitter (R29 derived-claim accuracy; R49 claim stronger than the implementation).

file: `migrations/0042_webhook_delivery.sql` — `ALTER TABLE organizations ADD COLUMN webhooks_enabled BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE`
title: `migrations` adds `organizations.webhooks_enabled` that nothing reads or writes
what_is_wrong: the migration declares an organization-level webhooks kill switch, but no model field, no route, and no code path in `enqueue_for_event` or `dispatch` consults it (R41: a declared capability with no backing path); it also defaults to `FALSE`, which reads as "off by default".

title: missing indexes for both hot queries; the one index that was added does not serve them
what_is_wrong: the claim query filters `status = 'pending' AND next_attempt_at <= now` ordered by `next_attempt_at`, and the listing filters `endpoint_id` ordered by `created_at DESC`, but the only index is on the extremely low-cardinality `status` column alone.

title: `_finish` dereferences a possibly-absent row and stores unbounded response bodies
what_is_wrong: `row = session.get(...)` is followed immediately by attribute assignment with no `None` check, and `response_body = detail` persists the full `response.text` of an arbitrary third-party response.

title: every new production export outside `signing.py` ships with no test
what_is_wrong: the diff adds `enqueue_for_event`, `deliver`, `run_worker`, `_acquire_lock`, `_claim_batch`, `_finish`, `WebhookEndpoint.to_dict`, `WebhookDelivery.to_dict`, and three HTTP routes, and the only tested symbols are `sign`, `verify`, `new_signing_secret`, `backoff_for`, `MAX_ATTEMPTS`, and `send_once` (RT6); there is no denial-path test for the deliveries endpoint at all, which is why the cross-tenant read shipped (RT8/RT10).

title: the existing tests are shaped so they cannot catch the defects in the code they cover
what_is_wrong: the signing test asserts only that the header *starts with* `sha256=` and never recomputes the MAC over `captured["body"]`, so it passes with the signature computed over entirely different bytes (RT5: the test claims to verify the signing primitive but never exercises verification against the wire form); `test_max_attempts_matches_documented_limit` asserts `MAX_ATTEMPTS == 5`, a restatement of the constant that pins the code to itself rather than to the doc; and the backoff parametrization hardcodes `2, 4, 8, 16` instead of deriving from `BASE_DELAY_SECONDS` (RT3).

title: `STATUSES` is declared but never enforced
what_is_wrong: the tuple is defined at module level and referenced nowhere; the `status` column is a bare `String(20)` with a string default.

file: `app/webhooks/models.py` — `WebhookDelivery.to_dict`; `docs/webhooks.md` — "returns the most recent attempts ... including the response status we saw and when the next attempt is scheduled"
title: `WebhookDelivery.to_dict` omits `created_at` that the docs imply
what_is_wrong: the serializer returns `next_attempt_at` but not `created_at` or `updated_at`, so a caller sorting or diagnosing by recency has no timestamp for when the attempt actually happened.

title: `EndpointIn.event_types` is unbounded in length and unvalidated in content
what_is_wrong: `list[str]` accepts arbitrarily many arbitrarily long strings, stored verbatim into JSONB.

title: the bytes that are signed are not the bytes that are sent
what_is_wrong: `sign()` HMACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` (default `", "`/`": "` separators, keys reordered) while the request body is produced independently by `client.post(..., json=delivery.payload)`, which serializes with httpx's own encoder (compact separators, insertion order), so the MAC covers a different byte string than the receiver gets.

title: signing secrets come from `random`, not a CSPRNG
what_is_wrong: the secret is built from `random.choice(_ALPHABET)`, i.e. the Mersenne Twister PRNG, which is seeded from predictable state and fully recoverable from ~624 observed outputs.

title: signature comparison is not constant-time
what_is_wrong: the HMAC comparison uses `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte, and this is the reference verifier the docs point customers at.

title: the timestamp header is not covered by the signature, so the documented replay window is unenforceable
what_is_wrong: the docs state the signature is `HMAC(secret, "{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}")` and that rejecting stale timestamps "stops a captured request from being replayed", but the implementation MACs the payload alone, leaving `X-Acme-Timestamp` attacker-mutable.

title: `list_deliveries` has no tenancy filter — cross-org read
what_is_wrong: the query filters on `WebhookDelivery.endpoint_id == endpoint_id` only and never joins to `WebhookEndpoint.org_id == user.org_id`, so any authenticated user can read any other organization's delivery history by incrementing an integer.

title: the signing secret is returned on every endpoint read
