title: the index set does not match the claim query
what_is_wrong: `_claim_batch` filters on `status` AND `next_attempt_at` and orders by `next_attempt_at`, and `list_deliveries` filters on `endpoint_id` and orders by `created_at`, but the only non-unique index is on `status` alone — a low-cardinality column.

title: `SECRET_BYTES` names a character count, not bytes
what_is_wrong: the constant is consumed as a length in characters, so the name overstates the entropy by asserting bytes where the value yields roughly 190 bits, and `test_new_signing_secret_has_prefix_and_length` cements the wrong meaning as a contract.

title: `list_deliveries` orders on a key with no total order
what_is_wrong: `created_at` ties routinely (a batch enqueue writes many rows in the same instant), so which rows fall inside the `limit` cut is undefined among ties (R57).

title: `enqueue_for_event` is declared `async` but performs only blocking work
what_is_wrong: the body is a synchronous SQLAlchemy session with no `await`, so awaiting it from `dispatch` blocks the event loop for the duration of the query while presenting an async contract.

title: `EndpointIn.url` has no length bound
what_is_wrong: the field accepts a string of any length into an unbounded `TEXT` column with no `max_length`.

title: `_finish` writes a response body on the success path
what_is_wrong: the successful branch persists the customer's 2xx body even though nothing reads it — `WebhookDelivery.to_dict()` does not expose `response_body`.

title: the bytes that are signed are not the bytes that are sent, and the timestamp is not covered by the MAC
what_is_wrong: `sign()` HMACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` (spaces after `,` and `:`, keys re-ordered) while `client.post(..., json=delivery.payload)` transmits httpx's own encoding (compact separators, insertion order), and the returned `timestamp` is never fed into the MAC even though `docs/webhooks.md` tells every customer the signature is `HMAC-SHA256("{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}")`.

title: `verify()` compares signatures with `==`
what_is_wrong: the recomputed digest is compared to the caller-supplied one with a short-circuiting `==`, which leaks the position of the first differing byte through timing (RS1).

title: signing secrets are generated with the `random` module
what_is_wrong: `random.choice` draws from the Mersenne Twister PRNG, which is not cryptographically secure and whose internal state is recoverable from a few hundred observed outputs.

title: the signing secret is returned by a read endpoint on every list call
what_is_wrong: `to_dict()` embeds `signing_secret`, and `GET /v1/settings/webhook-endpoints` returns it for every endpoint, directly contradicting `docs/webhooks.md` ("The response is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards").

title: `list_deliveries` has no tenant scope — any authenticated user reads any organization's webhook payloads
what_is_wrong: the query filters only on the path-supplied `endpoint_id` and never joins to `WebhookEndpoint.org_id == user.org_id`, while both sibling handlers in the same file (`list_api_keys`, `list_webhook_endpoints`) do filter by `user.org_id` (R3 — incomplete pattern propagation, security-relevant).

title: no SSRF control on the registered URL, and redirects are followed
what_is_wrong: validation is `parsed.scheme.startswith("http") and parsed.netloc`, which accepts plaintext `http://` (docs say HTTPS only) and any host including `127.0.0.1`, `169.254.169.254`, and internal RFC1918 names, and the worker then follows redirects from the customer's host to those same targets.

title: the migration's status CHECK constraint does not permit the status the code writes
what_is_wrong: the DB constraint allows `'failed'` while the Python `STATUSES` tuple and every `_finish` call site use `'failed_permanent'`.

title: the unique index on `event_id` makes fan-out to more than one endpoint impossible
what_is_wrong: uniqueness is on `event_id` alone, but `enqueue_for_event` inserts one row per matching endpoint for the same event.

title: the worker uses ORM instances after their session has closed
what_is_wrong: `_claim_batch` returns `WebhookDelivery` rows after `session_scope()` exits (commit expires every attribute under SQLAlchemy's default `expire_on_commit=True`), and `deliver` likewise reads `endpoint.signing_secret` and `endpoint.url` after its own `with session_scope()` block has closed.

title: `time.sleep()` inside an async coroutine blocks the entire worker
what_is_wrong: the retry backoff uses the blocking `time.sleep` inside an `async def` scheduled by `asyncio.gather`, so it stops the event loop rather than yielding.

title: `in_flight` is a non-terminal state with no reset path (R38)
what_is_wrong: rows are set to `in_flight` and committed, but nothing ever moves them back to `pending` if the worker crashes, is redeployed, or the coroutine raises before `_finish`.

title: the Redis lock is acquired non-atomically and can be leaked permanently
what_is_wrong: `get` then `set` is a check-then-act race, and `set` followed by a separate `expire` leaves the key with no TTL if the process dies between the two calls.

title: one bad delivery aborts the whole batch, and `batch` can be referenced unbound
what_is_wrong: `asyncio.gather` is called without `return_exceptions=True`, so any exception `deliver` does not catch (`httpx.InvalidURL`, `TypeError` from a non-serializable payload, the `IntegrityError` above, `DetachedInstanceError`) propagates and cancels the batch; and if `_claim_batch()` itself raises, the `finally` runs and then `if not batch` raises `NameError` on an unbound local.

title: `dispatch` swallows webhook enqueue failures
what_is_wrong: any failure to enqueue — DB error, the unique-index violation above, a `webhook_delivery` import-time error — is downgraded to a warning and `dispatch` returns the event id as if everything succeeded.

file: `app/events/dispatcher.py` — `WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES`; `docs/webhooks.md` — "An empty `event_types` subscribes the endpoint to every event type we emit"
title: `WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES` is a second, hardcoded subscription list that contradicts the documented contract (R42/R2)
what_is_wrong: the dispatcher gates enqueue on a three-element literal set derived by hand, while `enqueue_for_event` performs the real per-endpoint subscription filter — so an endpoint with `event_types: []` receives only those three types, and any new event type added elsewhere silently never reaches webhooks until someone remembers this set.

title: retry semantics contradict the documented contract on two axes (R29/R49)
what_is_wrong: the docs state a 4xx is permanent and that backoff is "exponential with jitter", but `deliver` retries every non-2xx identically for five attempts and `backoff_for` returns a deterministic `2**attempt` with no jitter.

file: `migrations/0042_webhook_delivery.sql` — `ALTER TABLE organizations ADD COLUMN webhooks_enabled BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE`
title: `organizations.webhooks_enabled` is added but never read (R41)
what_is_wrong: the migration declares a per-org feature gate that no code in the diff reads — not `create_webhook_endpoint`, not `enqueue_for_event`, not `dispatch` — and the ORM `Organization` model is not updated either.

title: signature and payload headers are written to the application log
what_is_wrong: the full outbound header dict, including `X-Acme-Signature` and `X-Acme-Timestamp`, is logged at `info` for every attempt, and `_finish` additionally stores the customer's full `response.text` in `webhook_deliveries.response_body` with no size or content bound.

title: `_finish` dereferences a possibly-`None` row
what_is_wrong: `row = session.get(m.WebhookDelivery, delivery_id)` is used without a `None` check, so a delivery whose endpoint (and thus, via `ON DELETE CASCADE`, whose delivery rows) was removed mid-flight raises `AttributeError`.

title: no rate limiting on the three new routes (RS2), and `limit` has no upper bound (RS3)
what_is_wrong: none of the new endpoints carries a rate limiter, and `limit` is bounded below but not above, so `?limit=100000000` is accepted.

title: async handlers perform blocking synchronous database work
what_is_wrong: every one of these is `async def` but uses the synchronous `session_scope()`/`session.query(...)` API, and `enqueue_for_event` is declared `async` while containing no `await` at all.

title: naive and timezone-aware datetimes are mixed, and the migration uses `TIMESTAMP` while the models declare `timezone=True`
what_is_wrong: `datetime.utcnow()` returns a naive datetime, `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` returns an aware one, and the DB columns are `TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE` while SQLAlchemy is told they are `WITH TIME ZONE`.

file: `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `_claim_batch` (`ORDER BY next_attempt_at LIMIT 100`); `app/api/routes/settings.py` — `list_deliveries` (`ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT n`); `migrations/0042_webhook_deli
title: the ordering keys have no total order, and the claim query has no supporting index (R57)
what_is_wrong: both queries order on a wall-clock timestamp that is not unique — every row of one `enqueue_for_event` call shares an identical `next_attempt_at`, and rows created in the same burst share `created_at` — so order among ties is undefined; and the only index is on `status`, while the claim query filters on `(status, next_attempt_at)` and orders by `next_attempt_at`.

title: the delivery worker, the enqueue path, and both serializers ship with no tests (RT6), and the one signing test cannot fail for the reason it claims (RT5/RT7)
what_is_wrong: the test file exercises only `sign`/`verify`/`backoff_for`/`send_once`; `test_send_once_posts_the_signed_payload` asserts only that the header *starts with* `sha256=` and that the timestamp is digits, so it stays green under every mutation of what is actually signed (the exact defect in the first finding); `test_verify_accepts_signature_produced_by_sign` round-trips `sign` through `verify` and is therefore tautological — it cannot detect that neither side matches the documented contract; and `FakeEndpoint`/`FakeDelivery` are hand-rolled doubles missing `event_types`, `active`, `status`, and an

title: `backoff_for` and `next_attempt_at` are written but never used to schedule anything
what_is_wrong: `next_attempt_at` is set once at enqueue and never advanced, and `attempts` is only persisted at the terminal `_finish` call — the retry loop lives entirely in-process, so the persisted state describes a schedule the code does not follow.

title: `SECRET_BYTES` names a character count, not a byte count
what_is_wrong: the constant is used as `range(SECRET_BYTES)` over a 62-character alphabet, so it counts characters; the name asserts an entropy quantity the code does not provide.

title: `WebhookDelivery.to_dict()` omits `endpoint_id`
what_is_wrong: the serialized delivery does not name the endpoint it belongs to, though the listing route is per-endpoint and a customer with several endpoints has no way to correlate rows if the shape is ever reused elsewhere.

title: `enqueue_for_event` is declared `async` but contains no `await`
what_is_wrong: the coroutine declaration promises the function yields to the loop, which it never does (covered structurally by the blocking-DB finding above, listed separately because the signature itself is the misleading part).

title: `docs/webhooks.md` describes constant-time comparison and a five-minute replay window as the customer's obligation only
what_is_wrong: the document instructs customers to use constant-time comparison and reject stale timestamps while our own `verify()` does neither, so the reference implementation contradicts the reference documentation.

title: the bytes that are signed are not the bytes that are sent
what_is_wrong: `sign()` MACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` (sorted keys, `", "`/`": "` separators) while the request body is produced independently by `client.post(..., json=delivery.payload)` using httpx's own encoder (insertion order, compact separators), so the digest never covers the transmitted bytes.

title: the signature does not cover the timestamp, so the documented replay window is unenforceable
what_is_wrong: `docs/webhooks.md` states the signature is `HMAC("{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}")`, but the code MACs the body alone and emits `X-Acme-Timestamp` as unauthenticated plaintext.

title: signature comparison in `verify` is not constant-time (RS1)
what_is_wrong: an exported signature-verification helper compares two MACs with `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte.

title: signing secrets are generated from a non-cryptographic PRNG
what_is_wrong: the secret that authenticates every outbound webhook is drawn from `random`, a Mersenne Twister whose internal state is recoverable from a few hundred observed outputs and whose seed is not secret.

title: unauthenticated-by-tenant delivery listing (IDOR)
what_is_wrong: the query filters only on `endpoint_id` from the path and never on `user.org_id`, unlike its sibling `list_webhook_endpoints` two functions above which does filter on `org_id`.

title: the migration's CHECK constraint forbids the status the code writes
what_is_wrong: the DB allows `'failed'` while both the model's `STATUSES` tuple and the only writer spell it `'failed_permanent'`.

title: the unique index on `event_id` makes fan-out to more than one endpoint impossible
what_is_wrong: uniqueness is on `event_id` alone, but `enqueue_for_event` inserts one row per matching endpoint for a single `event_id`.

title: `time.sleep` inside an async coroutine blocks the entire worker event loop
what_is_wrong: a blocking `time.sleep` sits in the retry loop of an `async def` that is run under `asyncio.gather` alongside up to `BATCH_SIZE = 100` siblings.

title: detached ORM instances are used after their session closes
what_is_wrong: both functions return or read mapped instances outside the `session_scope()` that loaded them, so every subsequent attribute access hits an expired/detached instance.

title: the dispatch lock is neither atomic nor owned, and can wedge permanently
what_is_wrong: `GET`-then-`SET` is a check-then-act race, `SET`-then-`EXPIRE` is two operations so a crash between them leaves a lock with no TTL, and the release deletes the key by name without proving ownership.

title: SSRF — the URL check accepts plaintext and internal targets, and redirects are followed
what_is_wrong: `startswith("http")` admits `http://` (which `docs/webhooks.md` says is rejected) and anything spelled `httpfoo://`, there is no check on the resolved host, and the delivery client follows redirects, so even an https public URL can bounce the request to an internal address.

title: the one test that could have caught the signing bug asserts only the shape of the signature
what_is_wrong: the test captures both `headers` and `body` but only asserts that the signature `startswith("sha256=")` and the timestamp `isdigit()`; it never recomputes the HMAC over `captured["body"]`, so the producer's signature is compared against nothing (RT1 — the double's captured value is never used to derive an independent expectation; RT5 — no test reaches the real verification path).

title: `in_flight` is a non-terminal state with no lease, timeout, or recovery path (R38)
what_is_wrong: rows enter `in_flight` on claim and leave it only on the success or permanent-failure path of `deliver`; no query anywhere selects `in_flight`, so a worker restart, an OOM kill, or any exception escaping `deliver` strands them permanently.

file: `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `deliver` (the `if 200 <= response.status_code < 300` branch falls through to the retry path for every other status)
title: 4xx responses are retried, contradicting the documented and correct behaviour
what_is_wrong: `docs/webhooks.md` states "a 4xx is permanent and we stop immediately", but the code retries a 400, 401, 404, or 410 the full five times.

title: the delivered payload carries no event envelope, so the documented deduplication is impossible
what_is_wrong: the HTTP body is the bare domain payload; `event_id`, `event_type`, and the occurrence time are stored in `webhook_deliveries` but never serialized into the request, while `docs/webhooks.md` instructs customers to "deduplicate on `event_id`" and to switch on the event type (R40 — producer shape versus the documented consumer contract).

title: the signing secret is returned on every list call and logged on every attempt
what_is_wrong: `docs/webhooks.md` states the secret "cannot be read back afterwards", but `list_webhook_endpoints` returns it via the same `to_dict()` used by the create route, and the delivery worker writes the full header dict — including the signature — to the application log at INFO on every attempt (R49: the claim is stronger than the implementation; RS4: credential material in a shipped artifact).

title: the three new routes have no rate limiting and no per-org endpoint cap (RS2)
what_is_wrong: the new mutation boundary accepts unlimited endpoint creations per org and the read routes are unthrottled, with no limiter applied and none of the existing routes in this file showing a shared limiter to adopt.

title: request parameters are unvalidated at the schema boundary (RS3)
what_is_wrong: `limit` has a lower bound but no upper bound, `url` is an unbounded `str` validated by hand-rolled `urlparse` logic deep in the handler rather than at the schema, and `event_types` is an unbounded `list[str]` never checked against the set of event types the system actually emits.

title: the event-type registry is hardcoded twice and the two lists cannot agree
what_is_wrong: the set of webhook-eligible event types is a literal in the dispatcher (three members), while the API accepts arbitrary strings and `enqueue_for_event` filters against `endpoint.event_types` — so the true delivered set is the intersection of two independently maintained lists, one of which is unwritten (R2 duplicated constant; R42 class-membership derived from a supplied list rather than from the defining primitive).

title: enqueue failures are swallowed, so events commit with no deliveries and no retry
what_is_wrong: the event row is committed in its own `session_scope`, then `enqueue_for_event` runs in a separate transaction whose every failure is caught and downgraded to a warning, with no outbox row, no retry, and no signal to the caller (R9 — the side effect is outside the transaction that made it owed).

title: naive `utcnow()` reimplements the module's own `_now()` helper and mismatches the column type
what_is_wrong: `models.py` already defines `_now()` returning an aware UTC datetime and `delivery.py` already imports `models as m`, yet `enqueue_for_event` hand-rolls a naive `datetime.utcnow()` (R1 — reimplementation of a helper present in the diff), while `_claim_batch` compares against an aware `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`; separately every migration column is `TIMESTAMP` (no time zone) although all five model columns declare `DateTime(timezone=True)` (R3 — the timezone-aware pattern applied in the model and not in the schema).

file: `migrations/0042_webhook_delivery.sql` — `ALTER TABLE organizations ADD COLUMN webhooks_enabled BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE`
title: `webhooks_enabled` is added to the schema and read by nothing (R41)
what_is_wrong: the migration introduces an org-level feature flag defaulting to FALSE, but no code in the diff reads it — `dispatch`, `enqueue_for_event`, and `create_webhook_endpoint` all proceed regardless, and `app/models/org.py` is not updated to map it.

title: the claim query reads then writes without row locking, and orders on a non-unique key
what_is_wrong: rows are `SELECT`ed and then mutated to `in_flight` in the same transaction with no `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` (R5 — read-then-write TOCTOU), and the ordering key `next_attempt_at` is not a total order: `enqueue_for_event` stamps every row of one fan-out with the identical timestamp (R57).

title: `_finish` dereferences a possibly-missing row and stores an unbounded response body
what_is_wrong: `session.get` returns `None` when the delivery has been cascade-deleted (the migration has `ON DELETE CASCADE` from `webhook_endpoints`), and `detail` carries the whole of `response.text` from a remote, attacker-controlled server straight into a `TEXT` column.

title: the entire delivery pipeline ships without tests (RT6)
what_is_wrong: the new production surface is `enqueue_for_event`, `_claim_batch`, `_acquire_lock`, `_finish`, `deliver`, `run_worker`, and three HTTP routes, and the only ones exercised are `send_once` and the signing helpers; `test_max_attempts_matches_documented_limit` asserts `MAX_ATTEMPTS == 5`, which is a restatement of the constant and cannot fail for any behavioural regression.

title: `docs/webhooks.md` documents behaviour the code does not implement (R29/R49)
what_is_wrong: four load-bearing claims are false against the code in the same commit — "Only `https://` URLs are accepted" (the check is `scheme.startswith("http")`), "backoff is exponential with jitter" (`backoff_for` has no jitter, and the parametrized test pins the exact deterministic values), "a 4xx is permanent and we stop immediately" (all non-2xx are retried), and "it cannot be read back afterwards" about the signing secret (`to_dict` returns it on every list call).

title: the delivery table lacks an index matching its hot query
what_is_wrong: the only index is on `status` alone, but `_claim_batch` filters `status = 'pending' AND next_attempt_at <= now()` and orders by `next_attempt_at`, and `list_deliveries` filters on `endpoint_id` and orders by `created_at` — neither is served.

title: `SECRET_BYTES` names a byte count but controls a character count, and a test pins the wrong property
what_is_wrong: the constant selects 32 characters from a 62-symbol alphabet (~190 bits), not 32 bytes, and the test asserts an exact total length, which locks in the current character-based generator and will red for the correct `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` fix.

title: `/webhook-endpoints/{id}/deliveries` is not scoped to the caller's organization
what_is_wrong: The query filters on the caller-supplied `endpoint_id` only and never joins `WebhookEndpoint` to check `org_id == user.org_id`, while the two sibling routes in the same file (`list_api_keys`, `list_webhook_endpoints`) both filter on `org_id` — the tenancy predicate was propagated to two of three new/adjacent read paths (R3, security-relevant).

title: the signature is computed over a different byte string than the one transmitted, and omits the timestamp
what_is_wrong: `sign` MACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` while `send_once` transmits `client.post(..., json=delivery.payload)`, which httpx serializes itself with default separators (`", "` / `": "`) and insertion order — so the signed bytes and the wire bytes differ whenever the payload has more than one key or any nesting; separately, `sign` never mixes the timestamp into the MAC even though `docs/webhooks.md` specifies the signed string as `"{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}"` (R40 producer-vs-strict-consumer, R48 two adjudicators of one predicate).

title: signing secrets are generated with `random`, not a CSPRNG
what_is_wrong: `random.choice` draws from the Mersenne Twister global instance, which is not cryptographically secure — 624 observed outputs recover the full internal state, and the state is shared with every other `random` consumer in the process.

title: `verify` compares signatures with `==`
what_is_wrong: The reference verifier compares an HMAC digest with Python's short-circuiting `==` (RS1) and performs no timestamp-freshness check, contradicting `docs/webhooks.md`, which instructs consumers to use a constant-time comparison and to reject requests older than five minutes.

title: the migration's status CHECK constraint does not contain the value the code writes
what_is_wrong: The SQL allows `'failed'` while both the model's `STATUSES` tuple and the only writer of a terminal failure use `'failed_permanent'` — the allowlist and its consumers were not synchronized (R18, R12).

title: `UNIQUE INDEX` on `event_id` alone permits only one delivery row per event across all endpoints
what_is_wrong: The uniqueness key is `event_id` alone, but `enqueue_for_event` inserts one row per matching endpoint with the same `event_id`, so a second subscribed endpoint collides (R57 — the de-duplication key is not the key the domain requires).

file: `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `deliver` (`endpoint = session.get(...)` used after the `with` block) and `_claim_batch` (`return rows` from inside `session_scope`)
title: ORM instances are used after their session closes in `deliver` and `_claim_batch`
what_is_wrong: With SQLAlchemy's default `expire_on_commit=True`, every attribute of an instance is expired at commit, so `endpoint.signing_secret` / `endpoint.url` inside `send_once`, and `delivery.attempts` / `delivery.payload` / `delivery.id` inside `deliver`, are read from detached instances with no session to refresh them.

title: `GET /webhook-endpoints` returns every endpoint's `signing_secret`
what_is_wrong: The single `to_dict` used by both the create response and the list response emits the secret, while `docs/webhooks.md` states "The response is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards" (RS4; R49 — the doc claims a control the implementation does not have).

file: `app/api/routes/settings.py` — `create_webhook_endpoint`, `if not parsed.scheme.startswith("http") or not parsed.netloc`; `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `httpx.AsyncClient(..., follow_redirects=True)`
title: endpoint URL validation permits SSRF, and the client follows redirects
what_is_wrong: The only check is a `startswith("http")` prefix test (which also admits `httpx://`) plus a non-empty netloc — plaintext `http://`, `http://127.0.0.1:6379`, `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`, and `http://[::1]` all pass, contradicting the doc's "Only `https://` URLs are accepted" (RS3, R49), and `follow_redirects=True` lets a public host 302 the signed request into the same internal space after validation.

file: `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `enqueue_for_event` (`payload=payload`) and `send_once` (`json=delivery.payload`); `docs/webhooks.md` — "delivery is at-least-once, so deduplicate on `event_id`"
title: the delivered body carries neither an event id nor an event type, so the documented dedupe key does not exist on the wire
what_is_wrong: The stored and transmitted body is the raw `envelope.payload` with no envelope fields, while the delivery row's `event_id` and `event_type` are never serialized into the request body or any header (R41 — a declared capability with no backing path).

title: `time.sleep` inside an `async def` blocks the event loop for the whole retry schedule
what_is_wrong: `deliver` is a coroutine gathered `BATCH_SIZE`-wide, but its backoff uses the blocking `time.sleep` rather than `await asyncio.sleep`, so a retrying delivery freezes the entire loop instead of yielding.

title: `in_flight` is a non-terminal state with no reclaim path, and the retry schedule columns are never written
what_is_wrong: Rows are marked `in_flight` and are only ever moved out by `_finish` on the success or exhaustion path; the loop retries in memory and never updates `attempts` or `next_attempt_at` between attempts, so a worker crash, deploy, or OOM strands rows in `in_flight` with no query anywhere that reclaims them (R38 clause 1).

title: the Redis lock is acquired non-atomically and released by name without ownership
what_is_wrong: The check-then-set pair is not atomic, so two workers can both observe an empty key and both proceed; the `set`/`expire` pair also leaves an un-expiring lock if the process dies between them; and the release deletes by key name without verifying the holder, so a worker whose batch outran the 60s TTL deletes a lock a *different* worker now holds (R51 — the decision is bound to a name, not to the object the operation acts on).

file: `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `run_worker`, the `try/finally` block and the trailing `if not batch:`
title: `run_worker` dies on the first exception and references `batch` before assignment
what_is_wrong: `batch` is assigned inside `try` but read after the `try/finally`, so any exception from `_claim_batch` propagates out of the `while True` (and a `NameError` would follow if it were caught later), and `asyncio.gather` without `return_exceptions=True` propagates the first delivery failure the same way — there is no `except` anywhere in the loop.

title: the event enqueue is fire-and-forget with a swallowed exception, after the event transaction has already committed
what_is_wrong: The enqueue runs in a *separate* `session_scope` outside the transaction that persisted the `Event`, and every failure is downgraded to a `warning` with no retry, no dead-letter, and no effect on the return value (R9, R4).

title: `WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES` is a second, hardcoded subscription gate that contradicts per-endpoint `event_types` and the docs
what_is_wrong: Two adjudicators decide one predicate ("should this event be webhooked") by different semantics — a module-level literal set in the dispatcher and the per-endpoint `event_types` filter in `enqueue_for_event` — and the doc states that an empty `event_types` "subscribes the endpoint to every event type we emit" (R48, R18, R49).

file: `migrations/0042_webhook_delivery.sql` — `ALTER TABLE organizations ADD COLUMN webhooks_enabled BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE;`
title: `organizations.webhooks_enabled` is added by the migration and read nowhere

title: signing secrets are generated with a non-cryptographic RNG
what_is_wrong: The secret is built from `random.choice(_ALPHABET)`, which is the Mersenne Twister PRNG seeded from a predictable state and explicitly not cryptographically secure, so an attacker who observes enough output from the same process (or brute-forces the seed) can reconstruct the generator and derive other tenants' secrets.

title: the endpoint list endpoint returns every signing secret
what_is_wrong: `to_dict()` includes `"signing_secret"` and is used by both the create route (where disclosure is intended, once) and the list route, so `GET /v1/settings/webhook-endpoints` hands back every secret on every call — directly contradicting `docs/webhooks.md` ("The response is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards").

title: deliveries can be read across organizations (missing tenancy filter)
what_is_wrong: The query filters only on the caller-supplied `endpoint_id` and never joins `WebhookEndpoint` to check `org_id == user.org_id`, while the two sibling routes in the same file (`list_api_keys`, `list_webhook_endpoints`) both filter on `user.org_id` — the tenancy predicate was propagated to two of three new/adjacent read paths and dropped on the third (R3, security-relevant, and RS3: an externally supplied identifier reaches a query with no ownership check).

title: unrestricted destination URL plus redirect-following makes the worker a read-SSRF proxy
what_is_wrong: The only check is `parsed.scheme.startswith("http") and parsed.netloc`, which accepts plain `http://`, and also `httpx://`, `http+unix://`, and any private or link-local host, while the client follows redirects and the response body is stored in `response_body` and returned by the deliveries API — so a registered endpoint can point at (or redirect to) `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` or an internal service and the caller reads the reply back.

title: the signature does not cover the bytes that are sent, nor the timestamp
what_is_wrong: `sign` HMACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` while `send_once` transmits the body produced by `client.post(json=...)`, which httpx serializes with compact separators and no key sorting — so the signed bytes and the wire bytes differ for any payload with more than one key or any non-ASCII value — and the timestamp is returned in a header but never fed into the MAC, so `docs/webhooks.md`'s stated construction `HMAC("{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}")` describes neither what is computed nor what can be verified (R40: producer wire shape vs the strict consumer that recomputes over the raw body

title: signature comparison is not constant-time
what_is_wrong: The HMAC comparison uses Python's `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte, instead of `hmac.compare_digest` (RS1).

title: the migration's status CHECK constraint rejects the status the code writes
what_is_wrong: The database permits `'failed'` while `STATUSES` and the only writer both use `'failed_permanent'`, so the three declarations of the same enum disagree (R3 incomplete propagation, R18 allowlist synchronization, R12 enum coverage) and the terminal-failure write is impossible.

title: the unique index on `event_id` alone makes multi-endpoint fan-out impossible
what_is_wrong: The uniqueness is declared on `event_id` by itself, but `enqueue_for_event` inserts one row per matching endpoint for a single event, so any org with two or more subscribed endpoints violates the index on the very first qualifying event.

what_is_wrong: `_claim_batch` returns `WebhookDelivery` instances after the `with session_scope()` block exits and `deliver` does the same for `WebhookEndpoint`, so every subsequent attribute read (`delivery.attempts`, `delivery.payload`, `delivery.id`, `endpoint.url`, `endpoint.signing_secret`) touches an expired, detached instance; the same defect appears at both sites, so fixing only `_claim_batch` leaves the second one live.

what_is_wrong: the diff adds `enqueue_for_event`, `deliver`, `run_worker`, `_claim_batch`, `_finish`, `_acquire_lock`, both models' `to_dict`, and three route handlers, and not one of them appears in any test — the covered slice is the one that contains none of the defects above.

title: the signature tests are self-consistent tautologies that cannot detect a broken signature (RT1/RT5/RT7)
what_is_wrong: `verify` is asserted only against a signature `sign` just produced, so any change to the signing scheme — including omitting the timestamp or signing bytes other than the transmitted body — keeps both green; and the send test asserts only that the header *starts with* `sha256=` and that the timestamp is digits, never that the signature validates over `captured["body"]`, so the producer/consumer divergence in the first finding is invisible (RT5: the test's call path never reaches the primitive it claims to verify).

title: ordering keys have no total order (R57)
what_is_wrong: both queries order on a wall-clock timestamp with no unique tie-break, and `enqueue_for_event` assigns every row of one event the *same* `next_attempt_at`, so ties are the norm rather than the edge case.

title: `_finish` dereferences a row that may not exist
what_is_wrong: no `None` check, so a delivery deleted by the endpoint's `ON DELETE CASCADE` between claim and finish raises `AttributeError`.

title: the only index does not cover the claim query's predicate
what_is_wrong: the claim query filters on `status` *and* `next_attempt_at` and orders by the latter, but the index has only `status`, whose selectivity collapses once most rows are `delivered`.

title: `attempts` is only persisted at terminal time
what_is_wrong: the retry counter lives in memory for the whole retry loop and reaches the row only via `_finish`.

title: the docs' retry table omits the fifth attempt
what_is_wrong: `MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5` means four backoffs after the first attempt, but the prose lists four delays alongside "at most 5 times" without saying which attempt each precedes.

title: `STATUSES` is declared and never used
what_is_wrong: the constant exists but the column default and all five writers in `delivery.py` use bare literals.

title: any authenticated user can read any organization's webhook deliveries
what_is_wrong: The query filters only on `WebhookDelivery.endpoint_id`, taken straight from the URL path, and never joins to `WebhookEndpoint` to check `org_id == user.org_id`.

title: the signing secret is returned on every read of an endpoint
what_is_wrong: `to_dict()` includes `signing_secret`, and it is the serializer used by `list_webhook_endpoints` (a GET), so the secret is readable forever by anyone with read access — directly contradicting `docs/webhooks.md` ("the response is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards").

title: signing secrets are generated with a non-cryptographic RNG
what_is_wrong: The secret is built from `random.choice`, i.e. the Mersenne Twister PRNG, which is seeded predictably and fully recoverable from a modest amount of observed output.

title: signature verification uses a variable-time string comparison
what_is_wrong: `verify` compares the recomputed digest with the supplied one using `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte (RS1).

title: the signed bytes are not the bytes on the wire, so no receiver can verify
what_is_wrong: `sign` HMACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` while the request body is produced independently by `client.post(..., json=delivery.payload)` (httpx's own compact, insertion-ordered encoding), so the MAC covers a byte string that is never transmitted (R40: producer shape vs strict consumer).

title: the timestamp header is not covered by the signature, so the documented replay window is unenforceable
what_is_wrong: The docs state the signature is `HMAC-SHA256("{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}")`, but `sign` MACs the body alone and returns the timestamp as an unauthenticated side value (R29: the doc describes a control the code does not implement).

title: the migration's status CHECK constraint does not admit the status the code writes
what_is_wrong: The constraint permits `('pending','in_flight','delivered','failed')` while `app/webhooks/models.py:STATUSES` and `_finish` use `failed_permanent` — the enum is spelled two ways across a strict consumer boundary (R40 enum-spelling clause, R2 semantic duplication).

what_is_wrong: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON webhook_deliveries (event_id)` permits exactly one delivery row per event, while `enqueue_for_event` inserts one row per matching endpoint.

what_is_wrong: Six new production functions are added and none is exercised; `MAX_ATTEMPTS` is "tested" only by asserting the constant equals 5, which pins the literal and not the behaviour it is supposed to govern (RT6, and RT8's vacuous-assertion shape).

title: an exception in `_claim_batch` kills the worker permanently and raises `NameError` on the way out

title: `_finish` dereferences a row that may not exist and can never return a row to `pending`
what_is_wrong: `row = session.get(...)` is used without a `None` check (a delivery deleted by the endpoint's `ON DELETE CASCADE` mid-flight yields `AttributeError`), and the helper accepts only terminal statuses in practice, so there is no path to reschedule.

title: the deliveries listing orders on a non-unique wall-clock column

title: `SECRET_BYTES` names a unit the code does not produce

title: docs describe an inspection response the API does not return
what_is_wrong: The docs promise "the response status we saw and when the next attempt is scheduled" for deliveries "belonging to your organization" — the org scoping does not exist (Critical above) and `to_dict` omits `created_at`, so "most recent attempts" cannot be ordered by the client (R29).

title: Signing secrets are generated from a non-cryptographic PRNG
what_is_wrong: The secret is built from `random.choice`, the Mersenne Twister, whose internal state is fully recoverable from 624 observed outputs and which is seeded from a low-entropy source shared by every other `random` caller in the process.

title: `verify` compares signatures with `==`
what_is_wrong: The recomputed digest is compared to the caller-supplied signature with a short-circuiting `==`, which leaks the length of the matching prefix through timing (RS1).

title: The bytes that are signed are not the bytes that are sent
what_is_wrong: `sign` MACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` while the request body is produced by httpx from `json=delivery.payload`, which serializes in insertion order with its own separators — two different byte strings for the same dict (R40, producer/strict-consumer divergence).

what_is_wrong: The doc states the signature is the HMAC of `"{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}"`, but `sign` MACs the body alone and returns the timestamp as an unauthenticated side value (R49: claim stronger than the implementation).

title: The signing secret is returned by the list endpoint
what_is_wrong: `to_dict` includes `signing_secret`, and `GET /v1/settings/webhook-endpoints` returns it for every endpoint on every call, directly contradicting the doc's claim that the create response "is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards" (RS4, R49).

title: `list_deliveries` is not scoped to the caller's organization
what_is_wrong: The query filters only on the path parameter `endpoint_id` and never joins to `WebhookEndpoint.org_id == user.org_id`, so any authenticated user can enumerate any other tenant's deliveries (R3: the sibling handlers `list_webhook_endpoints` and `create_webhook_endpoint` both scope by `user.org_id`, and this is the one place the pattern was not propagated).

title: Endpoint URLs are unvalidated and the client follows redirects — server-side request forgery
what_is_wrong: The only check is `parsed.scheme.startswith("http") and parsed.netloc`, which admits `http://`, admits any scheme merely beginning with those four characters (`httpfoo://`), and applies no host restriction, while the delivery client is constructed with `follow_redirects=True` (RS3/RS5).

what_is_wrong: The constraint allows `('pending', 'in_flight', 'delivered', 'failed')` while `models.STATUSES` and `_finish` use `failed_permanent` (R2/R3: the same enum is written out in three places — SQL, `STATUSES`, and the literals in `deliver` — and one copy drifted).

title: The unique index on `event_id` alone makes multi-endpoint fan-out impossible
what_is_wrong: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON webhook_deliveries (event_id)` permits exactly one delivery row per event, but `enqueue_for_event` inserts one row per matching endpoint.

title: `time.sleep` inside an async coroutine blocks the entire event loop
what_is_wrong: The retry backoff uses the blocking `time.sleep(delay)` inside an `async def` that is run concurrently under `asyncio.gather`.

title: ORM instances are used after their session closes
what_is_wrong: `_claim_batch` returns `rows` after the `with session_scope()` block has exited, and `deliver` fetches `endpoint` inside a `with` block then reads `endpoint.url` and `endpoint.signing_secret` outside it; with SQLAlchemy's default `expire_on_commit=True`, every attribute on those detached instances is expired and raises `DetachedInstanceError` on access.

title: One failing delivery kills the worker loop, and a claim failure raises `NameError`
what_is_wrong: `asyncio.gather` is called without `return_exceptions=True`, so any exception from any `deliver` propagates out of the `while True` body and terminates the worker; separately, `batch` is read after the `try/finally` but assigned inside the `try`, so if `_claim_batch` raises, `if not batch` raises `NameError` while handling the original error.

title: The signature test has no independent oracle, so it is green under a broken signature
what_is_wrong: The test asserts only that the signature header *starts with* `sha256=` and that the timestamp *is digits*, never recomputing the HMAC over the body it captured, and it substitutes hand-written `FakeEndpoint`/`FakeDelivery` classes for the real ORM models (RT1 (c)/(d): no independently written expected value, and the double's fields are not bound to the boundary's declared type; RT5: signature generation is a security primitive whose correctness the test only appears to cover).

title: `in_flight` is a non-terminal state with no reaper
what_is_wrong: Rows are set to `in_flight` at claim time and leave that state only when `_finish` runs on the success or exhausted path; a worker crash, a deploy, or the loop death above strands them there forever, and `_claim_batch` only ever selects `status == "pending"` (R38 mode 1: no failure exit, no bounded timeout).

title: The dispatch lock is not atomic and wedges permanently on a crash
what_is_wrong: The lock is a `GET` followed by a separate `SET` and a separate `EXPIRE`, so two workers can both observe an empty key and both proceed, and a crash between `SET` and `EXPIRE` leaves a key with no TTL that no code path ever clears (R38 persisted fail-closed wedge).

title: The retry ladder is not durable — `attempts` and `next_attempt_at` are never advanced

title: The three new routes have no rate limiting and no cap on endpoints per organization
what_is_wrong: No rate limiter is applied to any of the new endpoints and nothing bounds how many `WebhookEndpoint` rows an org may create (RS2).

title: `limit` has a floor but no ceiling

what_is_wrong: the retry backoff uses the synchronous `time.sleep` inside an `async def` that is run under `asyncio.gather`, so it blocks the event loop instead of yielding.

title: endpoint URL validation admits plaintext and internal targets (SSRF)
what_is_wrong: the check is `parsed.scheme.startswith("http")` — which accepts `http`, and also `httpx`, `http-foo`, any scheme with that prefix — with no host restriction at all, while `docs/webhooks.md` states "Only `https://` URLs are accepted" (R49: claim stronger than the implementation; RS3: validation deep in the handler rather than on the schema).

title: the one test of the signing path cannot detect that the signature is wrong

title: the dispatch lock is not atomic and expires mid-delivery

title: `in_flight` is a non-terminal state with no recovery path

title: naive and aware datetimes are mixed across the enqueue/claim boundary

file: `app/webhooks/models.py` — `STATUSES`; `docs/webhooks.md` — "Only `https://` URLs are accepted", "backoff is exponential with jitter", "a 4xx is permanent", "the response is the only place the signing

what_is_wrong: `STATUSES` is dead — no `CheckConstraint`, no validator references it — and five separate documented behaviours are contradicted by the implementation (each is covered by a finding above; recording them together because the doc, as a whole, describes a system that was not built).

title: signing secrets are generated with the non-cryptographic `random` module
what_is_wrong: The per-endpoint HMAC key is built from `random.choice`, which is a Mersenne Twister PRNG whose full internal state is recoverable from a few hundred observed outputs, so secrets minted in sequence are predictable from one another.

title: signature comparison in `verify` is not constant-time
what_is_wrong: The recomputed HMAC is compared to the caller-supplied signature with `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and so leaks the length of the matching prefix through response timing (RS1).

title: the bytes that are signed are not the bytes that are sent
what_is_wrong: `sign` computes the HMAC over `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` while `send_once` hands the same dict to `client.post(..., json=delivery.payload)`, and httpx serializes it with its own separators and insertion order, so the transmitted body is a different byte string from the one that was signed (R40 — the producer's wire shape does not match what the strict consumer, the customer's verifier, recomputes over).

title: the timestamp header is not covered by the HMAC, so there is no replay window
what_is_wrong: `sign` returns a timestamp but computes the MAC over the payload alone, so `X-Acme-Timestamp` is unauthenticated attacker-mutable data, and `verify` ignores the timestamp entirely — the replay defence `docs/webhooks.md` instructs customers to rely on ("reject requests whose timestamp is more than five minutes old — that window is what stops a captured request from being replayed") does not exist in the signed material.

title: the deliveries endpoint is not scoped to the caller's organization (IDOR)
what_is_wrong: The query filters only on `WebhookDelivery.endpoint_id == endpoint_id` and never joins to `WebhookEndpoint.org_id == user.org_id`, so any authenticated user can read any other tenant's deliveries by incrementing the path integer.

title: the signing secret is returned on every endpoint listing, contradicting the documented one-time disclosure
what_is_wrong: `to_dict` unconditionally includes `signing_secret`, and `list_webhook_endpoints` returns `[e.to_dict() for e in endpoints]`, so `GET /v1/settings/webhook-endpoints` hands out every endpoint's HMAC key — while `docs/webhooks.md` states the create response "is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards".

title: user-supplied URL is fetched with redirects followed and no scheme, host, or address restriction (SSRF)
what_is_wrong: The only validation is `parsed.scheme.startswith("http") and parsed.netloc`, which accepts `http://`, `httpfoo://`, and any host including `127.0.0.1`, `169.254.169.254`, and internal DNS names, and the delivery client then follows redirects, so even an https-looking public URL can bounce the request to an internal address (RS3 — validation is at the wrong depth and checks a prefix rather than the value's domain).

what_is_wrong: The code and `app/webhooks/models.py::STATUSES` both use `failed_permanent`, but the migration's CHECK list has `failed`, so the single write that records a permanently failed delivery is rejected by the database (R3 — the status vocabulary is stated in three places and propagated to only two).

file: `app/webhooks/delivery.py` — `run_worker` (`await asyncio.gather(*[deliver(client, d) for d in batch])`) and `_finish` (`row = session.get(...)` followed by `row.status = status`)
title: one failing delivery aborts the rest of the batch, and `_finish` dereferences a possibly-missing row
what_is_wrong: `gather` is called without `return_exceptions=True`, so the first coroutine to raise propagates and the remaining results are discarded; and `_finish` assigns to `row` without checking for `None`, which is exactly the exception that will propagate when a delivery's row was removed by the endpoint's `ON DELETE CASCADE`.

what_is_wrong: The enqueue is best-effort with no retry and no durable marker, and it runs *after* the event transaction has committed, so any failure — including the IntegrityError from the unique-index defect above — loses the delivery permanently while `dispatch` still returns `event_id` as if everything succeeded.

title: the signing secret is readable back through the list endpoint, contradicting the documented contract
what_is_wrong: `to_dict()` unconditionally includes the secret and both routes use it, while `docs/webhooks.md` states "The response is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards", so the documented control does not exist (R49: a claim stronger than the implementation).

what_is_wrong: The whole header dict, including `X-Acme-Signature`, is logged on every delivery attempt, and once the timestamp is bound into the MAC the logged pair is a complete, replayable authentication token for that payload.

what_is_wrong: The author validated one side of the range and not the other, so `?limit=100000000` is accepted and each returned row carries a full JSONB `payload`.

title: the delivery loop, claim, lock, enqueue and all three routes ship with no tests (RT6)

file: `docs/webhooks.md` — the "Retries" section and the "Registering an endpoint" section

what_is_wrong: Three claims are false against the code in this same change: "backoff is exponential with jitter" (`backoff_for` returns `timedelta(seconds=2**attempt)` with no jitter, as `test_backoff_grows_exponentially` proves by asserting exact values); "a 4xx is permanent and we stop immediately" (`deliver` retries every non-2xx status equally, up to `MAX_ATTEMPTS`); and "we POST every subscribed event" / "every event type we emit" (the dispatcher gates on three hardcoded types). The https-only and secret-readback claims are covered as separate findings above.

title: the scheme check accepts schemes that merely begin with "http"
what_is_wrong: `httpfoo://host/x` passes the prefix test and is stored, only to fail at delivery time with an unsupported-protocol error from httpx.

title: `SECRET_BYTES` names bytes but is used as a character count
what_is_wrong: The constant governs a count of alphabet symbols, not bytes, and `tests/webhooks/test_delivery.py::test_new_signing_secret_has_prefix_and_length` re-encodes the confusion by asserting `len(secret) == len(PREFIX) + SECRET_BYTES`.

what_is_wrong: `assert MAX_ATTEMPTS == 5` pins the literal against itself with no reference to the behaviour, so it reddens only when someone deliberately changes the constant and says nothing about whether five attempts are actually made.

what_is_wrong: `_claim_batch` filters `status = 'pending' AND next_attempt_at <= now` ordered by `next_attempt_at`, but the only index is on the four-valued `status` column, which cannot serve the ordering.

title: `ORDER BY created_at` has no unique tiebreak (R57)
what_is_wrong: Rows enqueued in the same `add_all` share a `created_at` to the microsecond, so their relative order is undefined and unstable between identical requests.

title: `response_body` stores the remote server's response unbounded
what_is_wrong: The full response text of a customer-controlled server is persisted with no length cap and no content-type check.

file: `migrations/0042_webhook_delivery.sql` — `endpoint_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES webhook_endpoints (id) ON DELETE CASCADE`

what_is_wrong: Delivery rows are the audit record of what was sent to a customer, and the cascade removes them when the endpoint is deleted.

title: `STATUSES` is declared and never used
what_is_wrong: Nothing in the change references the tuple, so it does not constrain the `status` column, the `_finish` call sites, or the migration's CHECK constraint.

title: the signature is computed over bytes that are never sent, and does not cover the timestamp
what_is_wrong: `sign()` HMACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` and never mixes in `timestamp`, while `send_once()` hands the dict to httpx as `json=delivery.payload` so httpx re-serializes it with its own key order and separators — so the signed string is neither the wire body nor the `"{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}"` that `docs/webhooks.md` tells the customer to reconstruct.

title: signing secrets are generated with `random`, not a CSPRNG
what_is_wrong: the secret is built from `random.choice(_ALPHABET)`, i.e. the Mersenne Twister, whose internal state is recoverable from a bounded run of outputs and which is not a cryptographic generator.

title: `verify()` compares the HMAC with `==`
what_is_wrong: the digest comparison is a short-circuiting string equality, and `docs/webhooks.md` in the same change instructs customers to use a constant-time comparison while the reference implementation we ship does not (RS1; R49 — a claim stronger than the implementation).

what_is_wrong: `to_dict()` unconditionally includes `signing_secret`, so `GET /v1/settings/webhook-endpoints` hands out the secret for every endpoint on every call, directly contradicting `docs/webhooks.md` ("the response is the only place the signing secret appears — it cannot be read back afterwards").

what_is_wrong: the query filters on the path-supplied `endpoint_id` alone and never joins to `WebhookEndpoint.org_id == user.org_id`, so `user` is authenticated but never authorized for the endpoint they name.

title: the migration's status CHECK does not permit the value the code writes
what_is_wrong: the code writes `"failed_permanent"` (and `app/webhooks/models.py` `STATUSES` agrees) but the constraint allows only `"failed"`, so the terminal-failure write is rejected by the database.

title: the unique index on `event_id` allows only one endpoint to ever receive an event
what_is_wrong: uniqueness is declared on `event_id` alone, while `enqueue_for_event` inserts one row per matching endpoint via `session.add_all(rows)`.

what_is_wrong: `session.get` returns `None` for a missing id and the next line assigns to it unconditionally.

what_is_wrong: `_claim_batch` filters on `status` *and* `next_attempt_at` and orders by `next_attempt_at`, but the only index is on the low-cardinality `status` column alone.

title: two tests cannot distinguish a correct implementation from a degenerate one
what_is_wrong: the first asserts a constant equals its own literal and constrains no behaviour, and the second passes for a `new_signing_secret` that returns the fixed string `"whsec_" + "a" * 32` — neither can redden for the reason its name implies (RT7).

what_is_wrong: the table stores the full event payload and the full remote response body for every delivery attempt, with no retention policy and no size bound anywhere in the change.

title: the HMAC is computed over bytes that are never transmitted, and the timestamp is not covered

title: signing secrets are generated with a non-cryptographic RNG

what_is_wrong: the test asserts `MAX_ATTEMPTS == 5` against a literal, and reads nothing from `docs/webhooks.md`, so it pins the constant to a second copy of itself rather than to the documentation it names.

what_is_wrong: `_claim_batch` filters on `status = 'pending' AND next_attempt_at <= now` and orders by `next_attempt_at`, but the only index is on the low-cardinality `status` column alone.

title: the signature is computed over bytes that are never sent, and omits the timestamp the docs say it covers
what_is_wrong: `sign()` HMACs `json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True)` while the request body is produced independently by httpx's `json=` encoder (unsorted insertion order, its own separators/`ensure_ascii`), and the MAC input omits the `"{timestamp}."` prefix that `docs/webhooks.md` tells every customer to include — so the signed bytes and the transmitted bytes are two different strings on two axes.

title: `/webhook-endpoints/{endpoint_id}/deliveries` has no tenancy filter

title: signing secrets are generated with `random`, not a CSPRNG
what_is_wrong: `random.choice` draws from the Mersenne Twister PRNG, which is seeded from a low-entropy state and whose internal state is recoverable from a modest run of outputs, so secrets are predictable rather than unguessable.

title: `verify()` compares signatures with `==`
